chunks.text: 3 Method After evaluating existing continual learning methods in our gynecological segmentation setting, we investigate how forgetting varies across different regions of the encoder–decoder architecture through two complementary analyses: (1) block-wise ablation analysis to measure the contribution of different encoder–decoder regions to segmentation performance, and (2) depth-constrained adaptation experiments in which parameter updates are restricted to specific encoder and decoder regions during sequential training. We consider a task-incremental segmentation setting in which each task corresponds to a distinct segmentation dataset with its own label space. We adopt a multi-head formulation with a shared encoder–decoder backbone and task-specific segmentation heads. We partition the U-Net architecture into depth-wise encoder and decoder blocks corresponding to different spatial resolution levels to analyze how segmentation performance depends on network depth. Encoder blocks are indexed from shallow to deep as E = { E 0 , E 1 , … , E n } , E=\{E_{0},E_{1},\dots,E_{n}\}, where E 0 E_{0} denotes the shallowest encoder block and E n E_{n} the deepest encoder block adjacent to the bottleneck. Decoder blocks are indexed from the bottleneck toward the output as D = { D n , D n − 1 , … , D 0 } , D=\{D_{n},D_{n-1},\dots,D_{0}\}, where D n D_{n} is closest to the bottleneck, and D 0 D_{0} is the final output-proximal decoder block. Each encoder block E i E_{i} corresponds to a decoder block D i D_{i} operating at the same spatial resolution level, as illustrated in Figure 1 . The bottleneck is treated as a separate intermediate region between the deepest encoder and decoder. Figure 1 : Overview of the proposed depth-constrained adaptation framework. Encoder–decoder blocks are progressively unfrozen from the bottleneck toward shallower stages during sequential adaptation.

Post-adaptation block-wise ablation is then used to examine how the new task depends on different encoder–decoder regions after continual adaptation. After training on each task in the sequential continual learning sequence, encoder and decoder blocks are ablated independently during inference, while the remainder of the network remains unchanged. For a selected block, output activations are zeroed before propagation to subsequent layers, and the resulting change in segmentation performance is measured. For a given block b b , the performance drop induced by ablation is defined as Δ b = D full − D b , \Delta_{b}=D_{\text{full}}-D_{b}, where D full D_{\text{full}} denotes the Dice score of the unmodified network and D b D_{b} denotes the Dice score after ablating block b b . To compare block importance across tasks with different baseline performance levels, we report the relative block contribution δ b = Δ b D full , \delta_{b}=\frac{\Delta_{b}}{D_{\text{full}}}, where larger values indicate greater reliance on the corresponding block. Repeating this procedure across all encoder and decoder blocks provides a depth-wise characterization of how segmentation performance depends on different encoder–decoder regions in a continual learning setting. We then perform depth-constrained adaptation experiments to examine how restricting updates to different encoder and decoder regions affects forgetting during sequential training. The network is partitioned into the same depth-wise blocks used in the ablation analysis, and selected subsets of blocks are frozen while the remaining regions remain trainable. During adaptation to a new task, only the task-specific segmentation head is initially trainable while the shared encoder–decoder backbone remains frozen. The bottleneck region is then unfrozen, followed by the deepest encoder–decoder block pair ( E n , D n ) (E_{n},D_{n}) . Additional block pairs are subsequently unfrozen progressively toward shallower network stages.

Because encoder and decoder blocks at the same depth are directly linked through skip connections and jointly process features at a shared spatial resolution, corresponding encoder–decoder pairs are adapted together throughout sequential training. This setup enables a controlled comparison of different adaptation configurations, ranging from updates restricted to bottleneck-adjacent regions to progressively broader adaptation across the network. Following sequential adaptation, we analyze how block importance changes across network depth using the same block-wise ablation procedure. Figure 1 provides an overview of the proposed depth-constrained adaptation framework. 4 Experimental Setup 4.1 Datasets (a) UMD (b) UT-EndoMRI (c) ECPC-IDS Figure 2 : Representative examples from the gynecological datasets used in the continual learning experiments. For UMD, contours correspond to UW (green), UC (cyan), MY (yellow), and NC (magenta). For UT-EndoMRI, contours correspond to UT (green) and EM (yellow). For ECPC-IDS, tumor annotations are shown in green, overlaid on fused PET/CT imaging. We evaluate continual segmentation using three public gynecological imaging datasets: the Uterine Myoma MRI Dataset (UMD) 16 , the UTHealth Endometriosis MRI Dataset (UT-EndoMRI) 12 , and the Endometrial Cancer PET/CT Image Dataset for Semantic Segmentation and Detection of Hypermetabolic Regions (ECPC-IDS) 22 . These datasets differ in imaging modality, anatomical targets, and annotation structure, thereby introducing realistic distribution shifts across tasks. UMD is a T2-weighted pelvic MRI dataset comprising 266 cases after preprocessing, with multi-class annotations of uterine structures including uterine wall (UW), uterine cavity (UC), myoma (MY), and nabothian cysts (NC) 16 . It represents a relatively stable and consistently annotated task.

UT-EndoMRI is a heterogeneous MRI dataset containing T1, T1-weighted fat-suppressed (T1FS), T2, and T2-weighted fat-suppressed (T2FS) acquisitions 12 . In this work, we use the 103 T1FS volumes that achieved the strongest performance in preliminary single-task experiments; comparisons across MRI modalities for UT-EndoMRI are provided in Appendix Table 7 . The dataset includes annotations for uterus (UT), ovaries (OV), endometriomas (EM), and cysts (CY), with partial label availability and considerable intra-dataset variability. ECPC-IDS is a multimodal PET/CT dataset comprising 134 cases and binary tumor annotations 22 . Compared to the MRI datasets, it introduces a distribution shift through multimodal PET/CT inputs and a simplified binary tumor segmentation objective. Figure 2 shows representative examples from the datasets used in the experiments, while Table 1 summarizes their main characteristics. Additional dataset distribution and preprocessing statistics are provided in Appendix Figure 8 . Table 1 : Summary of datasets used in the experiments. Dataset Modality Samples Labels Task Type UMD T2-MRI 266 UW, UC, MY, NC Multi-class ECPC-IDS PET+CT 134 Tumor Binary UT-EndoMRI T1FS-MRI 103 UT, OV, EM, CY Multi-class All datasets are preprocessed using the nnU-Net pipeline 6 , with minimal dataset-specific preprocessing to ensure consistent voxel spacing, orientation, and label formatting across tasks. To maintain a unified input representation, all inputs are formatted as two-channel volumes. For single-modality datasets, the modality is duplicated across both channels, while ECPC-IDS uses PET and CT as separate input channels. We formulate each dataset as a separate task in a sequential learning setting using the fixed task order UMD → ECPC-IDS → UT-EndoMRI . \text{UMD}\rightarrow\text{ECPC-IDS}\rightarrow\text{UT-EndoMRI}.

This ordering introduces challenging shifts in both input distribution and segmentation structure, progressing from a relatively consistent, fully annotated task to increasingly heterogeneous clinical settings with greater modality variation, partial annotations, and substantial anatomical variability. 4.2 Implementation Details All experiments are conducted using the nnU-Net framework 6 , its continual learning extension Lifelong nnU-Net 3 , and the MultiTalent nnU-Net framework 23 for joint multi-dataset training. These frameworks provide a standardized implementation for both sequential and joint training settings. Unless otherwise stated, all models use the default 3D full-resolution configuration and are optimized using stochastic gradient descent with a combined Dice and cross-entropy loss. During training, only data from the current task are accessible, with previous datasets revisited only in replay-based methods. Unless otherwise stated, conventional continual learning baselines are evaluated using the full three-task sequence. In contrast, the controlled depth-constrained adaptation experiments use a two-task setting comprising UMD and ECPC-IDS to isolate the effect of adaptation depth without interference from subsequent tasks. Architectural design, preprocessing, optimizer settings, and training schedules are kept identical across all methods to ensure fair comparison, with differences arising only from the continual learning strategy. Each task is trained for 100 epochs in both single-task and continual learning settings. For joint multi-dataset training using MultiTalent nnU-Net 23 , training is extended to 300 epochs to account for the increased data volume. All experiments are performed on an NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000 GPU with 24GB of memory. Following prior nnU-Net continual learning evaluations 3 , experiments use the standard nnU-Net 5-fold splits, with quantitative results reported for fold 0 unless otherwise specified.

All block-wise ablation experiments are conducted on the corresponding validation sets for the evaluated fold. 4.3 Evaluation Metrics Segmentation performance is evaluated using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC). To quantify forgetting, we report the average performance degradation across the continual learning sequence on previously learned tasks. Lower forgetting values indicate better knowledge retention, while negative values correspond to positive backward transfer. Quantitative results are reported as mean ± \pm standard deviation across samples in the evaluated dataset. 4.1 Datasets (a) UMD (b) UT-EndoMRI (c) ECPC-IDS Figure 2 : Representative examples from the gynecological datasets used in the continual learning experiments. Structure nnU-Net (Single) MultiTalent (Joint) UMD UW 0.8339 ± \pm 0.0920 0.6237 ± \pm 0.1082 UC 0.7421 ± \pm 0.1778 0.6546 ± \pm 0.1704 MY 0.6481 ± \pm 0.2868 0.3986 ± \pm 0.3412 NC 0.3875 ± \pm 0.3689 0.1618 ± \pm 0.2393 ECPC-IDS Tumor 0.8817 ± \pm 0.1402 0.8726 ± \pm 0.1441 UT-EndoMRI UT 0.6258 ± \pm 0.2553 0.4370 ± \pm 0.2281 EM 0.3419 ± \pm 0.3361 0.1647 ± \pm 0.2766 OV 0.1553 ± \pm 0.2448 0.0711 ± \pm 0.1130 CY 0.0273 ± \pm 0.0864 0.0158 ± \pm 0.0664 We first evaluate single-task, joint-training, and continual learning performance in our gynecological segmentation setting to establish reference performance levels and assess how existing methods perform under clinical heterogeneity. As shown in Table 2 , joint multi-dataset training frequently underperforms independent single-task training, particularly on UMD and UT-EndoMRI.

This suggests that variation across imaging modalities, anatomical targets, and annotation structures introduces representational interference even when all datasets are available simultaneously, indicating that continual adaptation across them is likely to pose an even greater challenge. Across all settings, segmentation performance on UT-EndoMRI is consistently higher for UT and EM structures than for OV and CY, suggesting that the latter remain considerably more challenging. Ovaries exhibit high anatomical variability and may be deformed, displaced, or absent in endometriosis patients, complicating reliable localization 12 . In addition, cyst annotations are extremely sparse, with only 17 annotated cases available, limiting the model’s ability to learn robust representations. Replay-based rehearsal provides the strongest overall retention, reducing the average forgetting from 0.7531 under sequential fine-tuning to 0.0815, while preserving substantially higher performance across both UMD and ECPC-IDS.

However, this improvement depends on storing samples from previously seen datasets, which may be impractical in medical settings due to privacy, storage, and data governance constraints. In contrast, regularization- and distillation-based approaches provide only partial stabilization. LwF reduces forgetting on ECPC-IDS relative to sequential fine-tuning, but substantial forgetting remains on UMD. EWC preserves the first task more effectively, achieving low forgetting on UMD (0.0830), yet fails to consistently retain intermediate-task representations, with forgetting on ECPC-IDS remaining high (0.6430). These trends suggest forgetting remains highly uneven across tasks despite these mitigation strategies, given the substantial heterogeneity in gynecological imaging. These observations motivate a deeper analysis of how forgetting emerges across encoder–decoder depth during sequential adaptation. 5.2 Block-Wise Ablation Analysis Across Encoder–Decoder Depth (a) (b) (c) Figure 3 : Block-wise ablation across sequential training stages. Restricting updates to the bottleneck produces almost no forgetting on UMD structures, but ECPC-IDS fails to learn effectively, indicating that bottleneck adaptation alone is insufficient for cross-task transfer. Expanding adaptation to include E 5 E_{5} and D 5 D_{5} still results in negligible forgetting, with forgetting remaining below 0.04 across all UMD structures (Table 6 ). A sharp transition emerges once adaptation extends to E 4 E_{4} and D 4 D_{4} . ECPC-IDS tumor performance increases substantially from 0.0669 to 0.7329 (Figure 4 ), while forgetting simultaneously rises to approximately 0.4 across multiple UMD structures. Extending adaptation further to E 3 E_{3} and D 3 D_{3} causes near-complete collapse of UMD performance, with DSC approaching zero despite only a subset of encoder–decoder regions remaining trainable. Figure 5 qualitatively illustrates this abrupt transition: segmentation masks remain visually stable when adaptation is confined near the bottleneck, but rapidly degrade as trainable stages expand toward E 3 E_{3} and D 3 D_{3} . We further repeat the block-wise ablation analysis after each adaptation configuration to examine how ECPC-IDS redistributes reliance across encoder and decoder depths under constrained adaptation. Table 5 and Figure 6 show that unconstrained sequential fine-tuning concentrates ECPC-IDS performance almost entirely in shallow encoder and late decoder regions, with maximal contribution scores at E 0 E_{0} ( 1.00 1.00 ) and D 0 D_{0} ( 1.00 1.00 ), while deeper encoder stages collapse to near-zero contribution. In contrast, restricting adaptation to bottleneck-adjacent regions produces a substantially broader contribution profile across deeper encoder and decoder stages. Under bottleneck-only adaptation, ECPC-IDS remains dependent on deeper encoder blocks ( E 3 E_{3} – E 5 = 0.62 E_{5}=0.62 – 0.85 0.85 ) and intermediate decoder regions ( D 3 D_{3} – D 5 = 0.54 D_{5}=0.54 – 0.99 0.99 ), while preserving low forgetting on UMD.

Expanding adaptation to include E 5 E_{5} and D 5 D_{5} still maintains substantial dependence across deeper network regions, rather than immediately collapsing toward shallow encoder stages. However, once shallower regions become trainable, the contribution profiles shift sharply back toward the shallow encoder and late decoder. For example, under the E 3 E_{3} – E 5 E_{5} + bottleneck + D 3 D_{3} – D 5 D_{5} configuration, ECPC-IDS again becomes almost entirely dependent on shallow encoder regions ( E 0 E_{0} – E 3 = 1.00 E_{3}=1.00 ), coinciding with near-complete forgetting on UMD. Similar concentration patterns persist as progressively shallower stages are unfrozen. These results suggest that constrained adaptation does not merely reduce forgetting by limiting the number of trainable parameters but also actively redistributes the new task’s representation within the encoder-decoder hierarchy, allowing deeper network regions to absorb adaptation while preserving shallow representations critical for previously learned tasks. To further examine whether forgetting can emerge under highly restricted adaptation, we perform an additional experiment in which all parameters are frozen except the earliest encoder block ( E 0 E_{0} ) and the final decoder block ( D 0 D_{0} ). Figure 7 shows the resulting behavior under different task transitions. During the UMD → \rightarrow ECPC-IDS transition, performance on all UMD structures collapses to zero, even though ECPC-IDS tumor segmentation reaches only a modest DSC of 0.1128. This indicates that severe forgetting can emerge even when adaptation capacity is highly constrained. The same behavior is observed during the UMD → \rightarrow UT-EndoMRI transition, despite both tasks using MRI inputs. UMD performance again collapses almost entirely.

This suggests that forgetting is not solely driven by cross-modality shifts, but can also emerge under within-modality adaptation when updates occur in shallow encoder and output-proximal decoder regions. These results are particularly notable because the overwhelming majority of network parameters remain frozen. Severe forgetting therefore emerges even when adaptation is restricted to a very small subset of shallow encoder and output-proximal decoder regions, further supporting the depth-dependent nature of forgetting in encoder–decoder segmentation networks. Existing continual learning methods showed limited ability to preserve previously learned tasks in this challenging clinical setting, motivating a deeper analysis of how forgetting varies across encoder–decoder depth during sequential adaptation. Through block-wise ablation experiments, we showed that segmentation performance depends disproportionately on early encoder and late decoder regions, whereas deeper bottleneck-adjacent stages contribute comparatively little. Using depth-constrained adaptation experiments, we further showed that restricting updates near the bottleneck largely preserves previously learned tasks, while extending adaptation toward shallower encoder and decoder stages leads to abrupt forgetting, even when only a small subset of parameters remains trainable. Post-adaptation analyses further revealed that different adaptation constraints lead to distinct depth-wise importance profiles, highlighting that adaptation can modify how segmentation performance depends on different encoder–decoder regions. These findings suggest that forgetting in continual gynecological segmentation is strongly influenced by where adaptation occurs within the encoder–decoder hierarchy. More broadly, they indicate that effective continual learning may benefit from adaptation strategies that explicitly account for the uneven functional importance of different network regions. Future work may build on these observations to develop continual learning methods that selectively preserve retention-critical representations while enabling efficient adaptation to new clinical tasks and distributions. Increasing rehearsal memory size consistently improves retention by preserving greater access to previously observed samples, although such approaches may be impractical in clinical settings due to storage, privacy, and data-sharing constraints. In contrast, EWC exhibits a strong stability–plasticity tradeoff. Weak regularization allows adaptation to later tasks but fails to preserve earlier knowledge, whereas stronger regularization substantially reduces forgetting at the cost of severely limiting adaptation to subsequent datasets, particularly ECPC-IDS. This behavior is evident in Figure 9 , where larger EWC regularization strengths preserve UMD performance while suppressing adaptation to subsequent tasks.
